Rules Animations Agents Diagrams Glossaries Formatting Logs

Diagrams

A visual language: the kinds of picture an agent draws in its replies, so the author reads at a glance what words would take a page to say. For each kind: what it shows, when it fits and when it does not, its parts, how it is drawn.

7 diagrams

7 diagrams
USEHand them to an agent 01Sequence diagram: who talks to whom 02State diagram: what moves a thing between its states 03Flowchart: what is decided where 04Timeline: what happened when 05Container sketch (C4): where the parts run 06Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links 07Status dashboard: where each part stands

USEHand them to an agent

Paste this into a project's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md: it is read at every start, so the agent draws its pictures this way without being told. The agents' guides hand these over too. To give one kind in a conversation, copy it with its Copy for an agent button.

Draw the pictures in your replies the way these diagrams say:
- Sequence diagram: who talks to whom: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/sequence.md
- State diagram: what moves a thing between its states: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/state.md
- Flowchart: what is decided where: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/flowchart.md
- Timeline: what happened when: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/timeline.md
- Container sketch (C4): where the parts run: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/containers.md
- Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/entities.md
- Status dashboard: where each part stands: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/diagrams/dashboard.md

01Sequence diagram: who talks to whom

The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change.

Fits when

  • Parts pass something along: a person, a browser, a server, a database, a job, an outside service.
  • The order matters: a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens where, and after what.
  • A fix changes the course: a step added, an event dropped, a call moved. Today beside proposed.

Not when

  • One part alone, nothing passed between: its states are a state diagram, its decisions a flowchart, its look a screenshot.
  • The order does not matter, only where the parts run or how the data links: a container sketch or an entity-relationship diagram.
  • The times matter more than who: a timeline.
  • Too many at once: more than five participants or ten messages. Split it in two, or say it in a table.
  • A change the author sees on screen: screenshots before and after say it better.

How it is drawn

  1. Participants: one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of the reading; the names stay short.
  2. Lifelines: a dashed vertical line under each participant.
  3. Messages: arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its arrow: 13:05 INSERT … SELECT, 403 plan limit.
  4. Today beside proposed (or before beside after, today beside made): two framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed out, a step added, a participant greyed.
  5. Around it: a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels.
  6. In the app's colours, and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words no smaller than the text around it.

Examples

In the author's words
  • Pictures that are clear to me; I'd like agents to make pictures of this kind in their messages: it makes them easier to understand. And especially the icons. (2026-10-13 15:29)
  • It makes sense to make one diagrams page, where we add diagrams, describe what they are, when they fit and when they do not: a visual language of sorts. This is a good example of a diagram for the course of events. (15:50)

# Sequence diagram: who talks to whom

The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each
other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or
a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change.

![Its parts: participants with an icon above the name, dashed lifelines under them, messages as arrows top to bottom; blue a request, green a success, red a failure, grey what stays the same](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_parts.svg)

## Fits when

- **Parts pass something along:** a person, a browser, a server, a database,
  a job, an outside service.
- **The order matters:** a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens
  where, and after what.
- **A fix changes the course:** a step added, an event dropped, a call moved.
  Today beside proposed.

## Not when

- **One part alone,** nothing passed between: its states are a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md), its decisions a [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md), its
  look a screenshot.
- **The order does not matter,** only where the parts run or how the data
  links: a [container sketch](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/containers.md) or an
  [entity-relationship diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/entities.md).
- **The times matter more than who:** a [timeline](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/timeline.md).
- **Too many at once:** more than five participants or ten messages. Split
  it in two, or say it in a table.
- **A change the author sees on screen:** screenshots before and after say it
  better.

## How it is drawn

1. **Participants:** one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A
   person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a
   cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside
   service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of
   the reading; the names stay short.
2. **Lifelines:** a dashed vertical line under each participant.
3. **Messages:** arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each
   with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or
   an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its
   arrow: `13:05 INSERT … SELECT`, `403 plan limit`.
4. **Today beside proposed** (or before beside after, today beside made): two
   framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only
   the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed
   out, a step added, a participant greyed.
5. **Around it:** a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of
   context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels.
6. **In the app's colours,** and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words
   no smaller than the text around it.

![S4, a plan limit: today the browser sends an error event to the tracker after the upgrade window; proposed, no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_plan_limit.svg)

## Examples

![U2, an upload retried: before, a passing 500 fails the export; after, the job waits and puts the file again, and the export is done](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_upload_retried.svg)

![D1, a deadlock in a cronjob retried inside the run: today an error event and the rows a run later; made, once more at once and no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_deadlock_retried.svg)

![D1, the same deadlock with no change proposed: the retry drawn as what would be done only if it grows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_deadlock_not_now.svg)

![E7, the exporter's upload: today a failed upload is an error event; proposed, retried up to 3 times, the file arrives, no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_exporter_upload.svg)

02State diagram: what moves a thing between its states

The states a thing has and what moves it from one to the next: a card's steps, a message's life, a job's run. Each state is a box; each arrow says what moves it.

Fits when

  • A thing has a few states, and the question is how it gets from one to another, or why it stays in one.
  • A state can be reached by more than one way, or left by a way that goes back.
  • A bug is a wrong state: stuck, skipped, or reached from where it should not be.

Not when

  • The order of calls between parts is the question: that is a sequence diagram.
  • One decision with its answers, no lasting state: a flowchart.
  • More than about eight states: draw the part that matters, and say the rest.

How it is drawn

  1. States: rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean: blue a step on the way, green the end that is wanted, orange one that needs a look.
  2. Transitions: the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words that move it (a click, an answer, a timeout).
  3. The start: a filled dot with an arrow into the first state.
  4. Around it: a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one line under it saying how to read it.
In the author's words
  • Add all five. (2026-10-13, as the note of 16:29 quotes it)
  • The new diagrams, I think, should go on the pages too, only in the same format as the other diagrams; and mind the arrows: take the ones the project uses. (16:33)

# State diagram: what moves a thing between its states

The states a thing has and what moves it from one to the next: a card's
steps, a message's life, a job's run. Each state is a box; each arrow says
what moves it.

![A sign-in card: from signed out through the code and the wait to saved; a refused code goes back for a new link, an unread token is shown in its window](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/state_sign_in.svg)

## Fits when

- **A thing has a few states,** and the question is how it gets from one to
  another, or why it stays in one.
- **A state can be reached by more than one way,** or left by a way that
  goes back.
- **A bug is a wrong state:** stuck, skipped, or reached from where it
  should not be.

## Not when

- **The order of calls between parts** is the question: that is a
  [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **One decision with its answers,** no lasting state: a
  [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md).
- **More than about eight states:** draw the part that matters, and say the
  rest.

## How it is drawn

1. **States:** rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean:
   blue a step on the way, green the end that is wanted, orange one that
   needs a look.
2. **Transitions:** the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words
   that move it (a click, an answer, a timeout).
3. **The start:** a filled dot with an arrow into the first state.
4. **Around it:** a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one
   line under it saying how to read it.

03Flowchart: what is decided where

The decisions one action goes through, in order: each question a diamond, each answer its own arrow, each outcome a box.

Fits when

  • One action branches: a click, a request or a job that does different things depending on what it finds.
  • The question is which way it went, and why: an outcome nobody expected.
  • A rule has cases, and every case must be seen at once.

Not when

  • A thing lives through states and comes back to them: a state diagram.
  • Several parts take turns: a sequence diagram.
  • More than about six questions: split it, or say it as a table of cases.

How it is drawn

  1. Steps: rectangles; the one that starts it darker.
  2. Questions: diamonds, a few words ending in a question mark, the words inside the diamond.
  3. Answers: the project's arrows, one per answer, each labelled (yes, no, or the value).
  4. Outcomes: boxes coloured by what they mean: green done, orange refused or spent, blue the way on.
  5. Left to right for the main way, down for the answers that leave it.
In the author's words
  • Add all five. (2026-10-13, as the note of 16:29 quotes it)
  • The new diagrams, I think, should go on the pages too, only in the same format as the other diagrams; and mind the arrows: take the ones the project uses. (16:33)

# Flowchart: what is decided where

The decisions one action goes through, in order: each question a diamond,
each answer its own arrow, each outcome a box.

![What Paste decides: a token, running, this link; each answer leads to its own outcome](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/flowchart_paste.svg)

## Fits when

- **One action branches:** a click, a request or a job that does different
  things depending on what it finds.
- **The question is which way it went,** and why: an outcome nobody
  expected.
- **A rule has cases,** and every case must be seen at once.

## Not when

- **A thing lives through states** and comes back to them: a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Several parts take turns:** a [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **More than about six questions:** split it, or say it as a table of
  cases.

## How it is drawn

1. **Steps:** rectangles; the one that starts it darker.
2. **Questions:** diamonds, a few words ending in a question mark, the
   words inside the diamond.
3. **Answers:** the project's arrows, one per answer, each labelled (yes,
   no, or the value).
4. **Outcomes:** boxes coloured by what they mean: green done, orange
   refused or spent, blue the way on.
5. **Left to right** for the main way, **down** for the answers that leave
   it.

04Timeline: what happened when

Events at their moments, from a log: one line of time, left to right, each event a dot with its time and a few words.

Fits when

  • A log tells it: times matter, and the gaps between them.
  • The question is what came before what, or what happened while something else waited.
  • One event went wrong among others that did not.

Not when

  • Who sent what to whom matters more than when: a sequence diagram.
  • The times do not matter, only the order of states: a state diagram.
  • Hundreds of events: pick the few that tell it, and say how many were left out.

How it is drawn

  1. The line of time: one grey line, left to right.
  2. Events: a dot on the line, a stem to its label, the time in bold above a few words. The labels go above and below in turn, so close events do not collide.
  3. Colours: blue for what went as it should, green for an end that is wanted, red for what went wrong.
  4. What went wrong gets a note of its own, in red, under its event.
In the author's words
  • Add all five. (2026-10-13, as the note of 16:29 quotes it)

Events at their moments, from a log: one line of time, left to right, each
event a dot with its time and a few words.

![A sign-in second by second: started, link opened, code typed, ended with the token unread, then Paste starting a new sign-in](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/timeline_sign_in.svg)

## Fits when

- **A log tells it:** times matter, and the gaps between them.
- **The question is what came before what,** or what happened while
  something else waited.
- **One event went wrong** among others that did not.

## Not when

- **Who sent what to whom** matters more than when: a
  [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **The times do not matter,** only the order of states: a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Hundreds of events:** pick the few that tell it, and say how many were
  left out.

## How it is drawn

1. **The line of time:** one grey line, left to right.
2. **Events:** a dot on the line, a stem to its label, the time in bold
   above a few words. The labels go above and below in turn, so close
   events do not collide.
3. **Colours:** blue for what went as it should, green for an end that is
   wanted, red for what went wrong.
4. **What went wrong** gets a note of its own, in red, under its event.

05Container sketch (C4): where the parts run

Which parts a system has, where each one runs, and what goes between them: the container level of the C4 model, drawn as a sketch.

Fits when

  • The question is where: which machine, which box, which service runs a part.
  • Something crosses a boundary: a laptop to a server, a box to the internet, and what goes across.
  • A newcomer needs the whole before any one part.

Not when

  • The order of the calls matters: a sequence diagram.
  • The data and how it links is the question: an entity-relationship diagram.
  • The inside of one part: its states or its decisions, a state diagram or a flowchart.

How it is drawn

  1. Where things run: dashed boxes with their names at the top left (a laptop, other machines, the internet).
  2. Parts: boxes inside them, a name and one line of what each is; the one the reply is about in blue.
  3. What goes between them: the project's arrows, grey, each with a few words.
  4. Names: the standard ones from the glossary of names (laptop, router, vps1, box), never a private host.

# Container sketch (C4): where the parts run

Which parts a system has, where each one runs, and what goes between them:
the container level of the C4 model, drawn as a sketch.

![Where the parts of a notes app run: the app, its folder and an agent box on a laptop; a router and agent machines; model and speech services on the internet](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/containers_notes.svg)

## Fits when

- **The question is where:** which machine, which box, which service runs
  a part.
- **Something crosses a boundary:** a laptop to a server, a box to the
  internet, and what goes across.
- **A newcomer needs the whole** before any one part.

## Not when

- **The order of the calls** matters: a [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **The data and how it links** is the question: an
  [entity-relationship diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/entities.md).
- **The inside of one part:** its states or its decisions, a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md) or a [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Where things run:** dashed boxes with their names at the top left (a
   laptop, other machines, the internet).
2. **Parts:** boxes inside them, a name and one line of what each is; the
   one the reply is about in blue.
3. **What goes between them:** the project's arrows, grey, each with a few
   words.
4. **Names:** the standard ones from the
   [glossary of names](https://vbarbarosh.github.io/rules/docs/glossaries.html#NAME) (laptop, router, vps1,
   box), never a private host.

06Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links

The kinds of data a system keeps, their main fields, and how many of one go with one of another: 1 to n, n to n, marked on each line's ends.

Fits when

  • The question is about data: where something is kept, what points to what.
  • A change touches a link: one becomes many, or a link goes away.
  • A newcomer reads the storage before the code.

Not when

  • Where the data lives (which machine, which service): a container sketch.
  • What happens to one record over time: a state diagram.
  • Every field of every table: keep the main ones; the schema is in the code.

How it is drawn

  1. Entities: a box per kind of data, its name in bold on a tinted band, its main fields under it.
  2. Links: plain lines, no arrowheads, a verb under the line (holds, has, linked in).
  3. Their ends, crow's feet: two short bars across the line where it is one, a three-pronged foot with a bar before it where it is many (one or more). 1 and n in bold beside them, for a reader who does not know the marks.
  4. Left to right in the order a reader meets them; a child under its parent.

The kinds of data a system keeps, their main fields, and how many of one go
with one of another: 1 to n, n to n, marked on each line's ends.

![A note's data: a note holds messages, messages are linked in subjects, a message has files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/entities_notes.svg)

## Fits when

- **The question is about data:** where something is kept, what points to
  what.
- **A change touches a link:** one becomes many, or a link goes away.
- **A newcomer reads the storage** before the code.

## Not when

- **Where the data lives** (which machine, which service): a
  [container sketch](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/containers.md).
- **What happens to one record over time:** a [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Every field of every table:** keep the main ones; the schema is in the
  code.

## How it is drawn

1. **Entities:** a box per kind of data, its name in bold on a tinted band,
   its main fields under it.
2. **Links:** plain lines, no arrowheads, a verb under the line (holds, has,
   linked in).
3. **Their ends, crow's feet:** two short bars across the line where it is
   one, a three-pronged foot with a bar before it where it is many (one or
   more). **1** and **n** in bold beside them, for a reader who does not
   know the marks.
4. **Left to right** in the order a reader meets them; a child under its
   parent.

07Status dashboard: where each part stands

A RAG status dashboard (red, amber, green): the state of many parts at once, each a tile coloured by its state. Big numbers on top, the tiles grouped below, the gaps gathered at the end.

Fits when

  • The question is where things stand: many parts, each in place, stale or missing.
  • The reader must find the gaps fast: a project's checks, a release, an audit of what is covered.
  • The same view is read again later, and the colours show what moved.

Not when

  • One thing and its states over time: a state diagram.
  • What happened in what order: a timeline or a sequence diagram.
  • A few parts only: a sentence or a list says it; a dashboard needs enough tiles to scan.

How it is drawn

  1. The key: green in place and checked, amber stale or unchecked, red missing or failed, in one line under the title.
  2. KPI cards: three or four big numbers on top, each a word of what it counts and a line of context, coloured like the worst it stands for.
  3. The status board: a panel per area, its name and a line of what it holds; a tile per part, its name in bold and its state in its colour.
  4. The gaps: the amber and red tiles again, gathered in a panel at the end, so the reader does not hunt for them.
  5. Real states only: a tile's word says why it has its colour ("1 failed", "no test"), never just "bad".
In the author's words
  • Let's add it to the diagrams too, but first make a few sketches. (2026-10-14 13:45, of a status dashboard)
  • Sketch: A, the full dashboard. (13:49)
